title: Hydrodynamic description of proliferating active matter
authors: Nathan Silvano, Emilio Hernandez-Garcia, Cristóbal López
abstract: We develop a continuum theory for proliferating active matter starting from a microscopic stochastic model of self-propelled particles undergoing birth, death, and nonlocal competition. Beginning from the master equation, we derive mean-field evolution equations for the particle density and polarization fields and close the resulting hierarchy through a von Mises ansatz, providing a coupled hydrodynamic description applicable to a broad class of proliferating active systems. As an application, we study the recently introduced Active Brownian Bug model, in which the form of flocking emerges despite the absence of explicit alignment interactions. Linear stability analysis predicts both Turing and Hopf instabilities, whose analytical thresholds agree with numerical simulations. The continuum model reproduces the principal dynamical regimes of the underlying particle system, including homogeneous states, stationary periodic clusters, and coherently propagating flocking states. These results establish a general continuum framework for proliferating active matter and provide a physical interpretation of collective motion driven by the interplay between activity and population dynamics.
summary: This paper establishes a general continuum hydrodynamic framework for complex proliferating active matter by deriving mean-field equations from a detailed lattice master equation. Using the von Mises ansatz, they successfully model collective behaviors like flocking and predict pattern formation instabilities (Turing/Hopf) that match numerical simulations.
main_problem: Developing a general continuum theory for proliferating active matter that incorporates self-propulsion, birth, death, and nonlocal competition.
main_result: The derived hydrodynamic framework successfully reproduces key dynamical regimes, including Turing and Hopf instabilities, confirming its applicability to diverse active systems.
method: The authors derive mean-field evolution equations from a microscopic master equation by taking the continuum limit and employing a von Mises ansatz closure for angular correlations.
model_or_system: The model describes self-propelled particles on a lattice undergoing stochastic processes (birth, death, competition) alongside directional hopping. The dynamics are mapped onto coupled hydrodynamic equations for particle density and polarization fields.

important_parameters: Net growth rate ($\mu$), Péclet number ($Pe$), Diffusion coefficients ($D_T, D_R$).
main_assumptions: The primary approximations include the mean-field factorization of averages and the use of the von Mises ansatz to close the resulting hierarchy of moment equations.
figures_summary: Figure D1 shows simulation results for a quasi-one-dimensional system, demonstrating hysteretic behavior (bistability) when sweeping parameters like the growth rate ($\mu$) across instability lines for specific Péclet numbers ($Pe=5$ and $Pe=7.5$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the microscopic lattice model via a master equation to deriving mean-field continuum equations, applying the von Mises closure to obtain coupled hydrodynamic equations for density ($ho$) and polarization ($P$), and finally analyzing these equations in simplified 1D systems to study pattern formation and bistability.
why_interesting: While focused on classical active matter, the rigorous derivation of macroscopic field theories from microscopic stochastic rules, coupled with stability analysis (Turing/Hopf), mirrors techniques used in modeling non-equilibrium quantum many-body dynamics or open quantum systems far from equilibrium.
